titleStmt.title: Interview with Harry B. Duke, Undated
titleStmt.author: Ronald M. Harwood

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Harry B. Duke was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: I enlisted in the U.S. Marine Corps. I enlisted in January, 1942, as soon as I could, right after Pearl Harbor, and went to Parris Island as my boot camp. And after boot camp I went to sea school, West Virginia, where we were getting ready, and after finishing sea school we went aboard the USS South Dakota. The South Dakota type battleship was brand-new, there was five in that class, and it was kept a secret for a long time. In fact they didn't reveal the name of the USS South Dakota until after the war; we were known as Battleship X the whole time. During the Pacific, with the battleship, I earned eight battle stars for the eight different actions that we were in. The big ones were the air/sea battle of Santa Crue [ph] Island, where the South Dakota was credited with shooting down 32 Japanese bombers, torpedo bombers. The next battle was only three weeks later. We were in the battle of Sabo Island, the third battle of Sabo Island, which was credited with keeping the Japanese from retaking Guadalcanal. We got hit pretty bad in the battle of Sabo Island. We also took a 500-pound bomb in the air/sea battle of Santa Crue Island so we had to go back to the States. We went into Bremerton, Washington and when we got all repaired we headed for the Atlantic, which we joined the British fleet up at ____ ____ ____. Our mission was to try to get the German battleship VonTrepid, which was a (pocket) battleship, that they only had left since the (?Graft Bay?) had been sunk. But we couldn't get them. They were hidden in the fiords, what they called, in Norway, and the only way they did get that was a two-man submarine that could go underneath there and get it. But anyway, we had a good trip with the English, and the best part about it, we were trading our cans of beer for their rum.

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: [Laughs].

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: After that we went back to the Pacific, and as soon as we got to Hawaii I got transferred. And they put me on the -- in Hawaii, until I got a ship back, a ship back to Camp LeJeune, where I was field artillery. When I got orders to Camp Pendleton, I reported into Camp Pendleton -- I can't give you the date -- but did a little bit of wartime training. And then the day that we were all moved out, just as we was going to get into the truck to take us to the embarcation, they called my name and they said, "You have had sea duty." "Yes, I was aboard the South Dakota." So they pulled me out and sent me to Camp Elliott, to transport quartermaster, which meant that there was an officer and an enlisted aboard every troop carrier and every supply carrier -- AKA and APA. Our job was to make sure that they was equally balanced for all the supplies, getting jeeps and tanks and everything in there. And I'm proud to say that I made an excellent transport man. So I was sent back to Hawaii, and I think it was a little town called Aiea, and I was waiting and waiting until the war ended. Then the worst part of my duty, I had to come back to the States on an LST --

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: [Laughs].

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: [Laughs]. That is no fun. I wish my number hadn't been that quick. Anyway, you understand.

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: [Laughs]. Yes.

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: But I come back and I went to -- my term was about up, I went to Rhode Island, to the Navy -- the Navy -- whatever it was ...

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: Newport --

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: Newport, Rhode Island, yes, and waiting for a discharge. And I was supposed to be discharged on January the 3rd, when I came down with tonsillitis and they put me in the hospital and took my tonsils out. But they did let me go January the 10th. That ended my World War II.

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: I have a question. What was your duties aboard the --

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: The duties aboard the South Dakota?

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: Mostly we were a landing crew if we had to land. But we had a communication orderly, admiral's orderly, captain's orderly, time orderly and -- you know, one of my specialties was time orderly where you had to ring the bell.

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: [Laughs].

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: And you had to ring it properly or everybody got mixed up. But that was most of our duty.

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: Did you qualify as a gunner?

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: In the Marine Corps?

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: I mean in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: Oh, yeah. At first we were put on the five-inch mount and I was a pointer. And the two marine mounts -- they had two of us, two sections of marines on the five-inch mount -- were the only two that got "E" -- excellent in practice. They would send a plane up with a big trailer and a big tugboat with a big trailer ... and I have a friend of mine, Charles Ingram, who was on the Rochester, and they're credited with shooting the tug instead of the trailer.

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: [Laughs].

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: And sank it -- they did. Yeah, and I was allowed to wear a symbol on my uniform, a circle with a thing in it that showed you pointing. Also we were supposed to get five dollars in pay every month, extra. But it turned out that before we got in battle, we were put on the 20th millimeter mount and there was a loaded gunner on the second 20 millimeter, on the fourth star -- I mean starboard 20-millimeter mount.

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: Oh, yes; okay.

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: They had an inscription on there. They had 20-millimeter ammunition, was given to me by Colonel Wally Williams and he had it inscribed with my name and the gun mount and everything else. Very good, I enjoyed that. That's about all we did. Oh, we had loading party, you know, loading and unloading. The biggest thing was the [somebody], they would come over the loudspeaker, "We need ten sailors for a working party," and two minutes later: "Delay that; just send a couple marines."

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: [Laughs].

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: So we always had good fun with them.

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: What did you do after World War II?

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: I went to my home town and a friend of mine who I joined the Marine Corps initially with, when I went back on January the 2nd we rode out to Parris Island and they called my name out and they said, "You are not going anywhere, because you're not an American citizen." So I had to go back home and get my father's citizenship papers and go back the next day. So I never saw my buddy the whole time after that. We joined together and when we got out we both came to Western Carolina -- which is now Western Carolina University -- but when we were down here it was Western Carolina Teachers School. And I was a member of the football team and I was a member of the only championship football team Western Carolina ever had. We won in 1949, we won the North Bay Conference championship. After graduation I taught at Old Town School in Winston-Salem, a county school, and it was nice, but no pay. They don't like to pay their teachers. So I was teaching two people whose father was a supervisor at Western Electric. He said, "If you want to come to work for us, I'll double what you're making here." Well, who's going to refuse that?

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: [Laughs].

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: So I went with Western Electric and I was assigned as a cost estimator, and my job was to estimate what it cost to make a Nike missile; my project was a Nike missile that they were working on. And that was good for two years, but I did not like sitting behind a desk for two years. So I read in the paper where the Marine Corps was opening a recruit station, and they were looking for people in Winston-Salem, and that was a reserve unit. And I went down just to say hello. "Oh, could we use you" you know, and "We'll do this" and "We'll do that" and "You have so many kids and they'll be taken care of," and everything else. Well, believe it or not, I signed up and almost scared my wife to death. She was in the hospital having a baby and I reported to her with my uniform on and she almost fainted again.

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: [Laughs].

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: But anyway, I stayed there for a year or so and found out that every marine reserve unit has to have a newspaper. I knew nothing about newspapers except as far as just reading them. But they read in my record that I was a college graduate so they figured I could at least spell a little bit. So we named the paper "The Gravel Cruncher," and it was run off by a mimeograph machine; just tits and tats about what was going on in the service. And I got worried and told the Navy, "I'd like to do this but I'd like to know more about journalism." So they sent me to Chicago to journalism school. And I was thinking I'd get back there, but I got orders for Japan. Now, I had to go fight them orders because I had a retarded son that was giving us a lot of problems. So they sent us to Camp LeJeune. And when we got to Camp LeJeune we told them about our son who was retarded but very high -- running all over the place, and they were willing to build a fence around the Cape Cod unit we had down there. And this was fine, but I got orders for Japan again, and they said I couldn't get out of this one. So my wife moved to [Kingston] and we had enough backing to get my son into Caswell Training School for people in that condition. So she stayed with them the 18 months, almost two years while I served at Iwakuni, Japan and of course I was -- after it all ended up, I would end up as the editor of [?The Storyteller?], which was the paper. And during the tour there was a movie director that came down and asked if anybody wanted to take leave, that they would pay them 10 dollars a day to act in the movie "The Last Voyage" with Robert stack, Dorothy Malone, George Saunders, Woody Hays -- all of that. And I took two weeks leave, which I had at the time, and went and we were used as extras. Because they had named this ship -- it was the old Ile de France, the old troopship Ile de France, and they were taking it, towing it to Tokyo for scrap,and he was headed back from somewhere and spotted it and said, "We want that ship." Okay. [Interview interrupted for coffee break]

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: So from Iwakuni I was transferred to Cherry Point, and became a member of the [windsock] staff and served there, ending up as an editor after several transfers. And from there -- when did I go to Viet Nam? Oh, so after Japan, yeah, I came back -- that's right -- and I went to Cherry Point and stayed there three years and then got orders for Marine Corps Sig -- Marine Corps Headquarters District in Atlanta, where I was editor of the Dixie Digest. After three years there, I got my orders for Viet Nam and was ordered to Da Nang CIB, Command Information Bureau. Da Nang, yeah. We were then classified as combat correspondents -- photographers, radio people, writers and all that. And my job was to escort visiting newspeople from all over the country to various action spots where they could get their news to send home. We stayed there in a French compound, which belonged to the French when they were over there, and we had a nice little room right on the beach, the Da Nang River, and I used to love to go fishing and catch red snapper. That was the first six months. I was called the Escort NCO and I went on a couple of trips -- we had a fellow named Shad, who we called the shotgun provider. He was fully equipped to take care, you know, of a company ___, and I had the chance to go up near the DMZ to a [kak] out there, a ____ company, they had a captain Dick Arnold. While we were there, a little boy riding a water buffalo, the buffalo stepped on a mine and killed that ____. We got the call and we were ready to go out, but the captain ordered me to stay back because of my age. I was getting into -- I was well into 38 or 40 then, so I didn't go. But when they brought him back, I saw them fixing him up and all that. And that was for the first six months. Then they put me on as editor of the Sea Tide, the newspaper for the marines, all the units, and during the six months of that duty, the newspaper -- the newspaper won the Navy -- Pentagon Navy award for the best newspaper. That fellow Dick Arnold I mentioned, he gets most of the credit because he showed me how to make a new format that would please every one of the units in Viet Nam that was saying that "We never get no publicity." So from there I came to Camp Pendleton where I took over as the information chief. I stayed there for about two years, a year and a half, two years, when somebody says I had orders for Viet Nam and I said, No way, I wasn't going back to Viet Nam, and I put in for my retirement papers. And I came back to [Cullawee].

sp.speaker: Ronald M. Harwood
sp.p: Well, thank you, Harry, that was very interesting, and I'm sure that will work well.

sp.speaker: Harry B. Duke
sp.p: Well, good; I hope so.
[End of interview]
